title: How to Run NVIDIA Cosmos 3 on Local AI Devices Using Hugging Face Diffusers | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA shows how to run its Cosmos 3 Nano world foundation model on consumer GeForce RTX GPUs with as little as 12 GB VRAM by streaming transformer weights from system RAM via a Hugging Face Diffusers adapter, plus an FP8 checkpoint. Benchmarks show it works but is slow: 720p text-to-video takes ~44 minutes on an RTX 5070 versus ~17 minutes on an RTX 5090, and hosts carried ~128 GB of system RAM.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's Cosmos-Framework offloading package runs the Cosmos 3 Nano world foundation model on GPUs with as little as 12 GB of VRAM by keeping model weights in system RAM and moving each transformer block to the GPU only when needed.
insights.speaker: Atharva Joshi
insights.so_what: Pushes physical-AI video generation onto mainstream consumer GPUs, widening NVIDIA's developer base beyond data-center hardware.

insights.claim: Weight streaming trades GPU memory for higher system RAM use and PCIe transfer load, and does not deliver interactive latency.
insights.speaker: Atharva Joshi
insights.so_what: Local video-gen shifts bottlenecks to DRAM capacity and PCIe bandwidth, a tailwind for high-capacity PC memory.
insights.quote: Note that this approach does not provide interactive latency or stream weights directly from disk during inference.

insights.claim: All tested consumer-GPU hosts for Cosmos 3 Nano local generation had approximately 128 GB of system RAM, though NVIDIA says this is not a measured minimum.
insights.speaker: Atharva Joshi
insights.so_what: The real cost of running world models locally includes a large DRAM footprint, relevant to memory demand from AI PCs and workstations.

insights.claim: The Cosmos adapter computes the understanding pathway once for fixed conditioning and reuses each streamed block across both classifier-free guidance predictions to avoid repeated weight transfers.
insights.speaker: Atharva Joshi
insights.so_what: Shows software scheduling, not just hardware, determines whether large models fit on small GPUs.

insights.claim: Cosmos 3 is an open omnimodal world foundation model for physical AI with separate understanding and generation pathways inside one transformer, supporting text-, image- and video-to-video, sound, action and control-guided generation through one Diffusers pipeline.
insights.speaker: Atharva Joshi
insights.so_what: Open multimodal world models with action outputs are NVIDIA's play to own the robotics/physical-AI software stack that drives GPU demand.

insights.claim: Cosmos 3 Nano can generate robot action outputs from a conditioning video in a policy mode, e.g. using the bridge_orig_lerobot domain, with action runs completing in roughly 38-66 seconds on an RTX 5070.
insights.speaker: Atharva Joshi
insights.so_what: Action generation is far cheaper than video generation, making robot-policy experimentation feasible on consumer cards.

insights.claim: The Cosmos 3 Nano FP8 checkpoint uses W8A16 for the first three and last three denoising steps and W8A8 for the middle steps, while attention stays in BF16 SDPA, so the pipeline is not fully FP8.
insights.speaker: Atharva Joshi
insights.so_what: Mixed-precision schedules are how model vendors squeeze consumer hardware; full low-precision attention remains unsolved here.
insights.quote: Note that attention remains BF16 SDPA; the entire pipeline does not run in FP8.

insights.claim: On a 12 GB RTX 5070, the FP8 checkpoint cut 720p text-to-video time from 2,624.9 s to 2,235.7 s (about 15%) and peak memory from 9.94 GiB to 9.16 GiB, in single-run measurements.
insights.speaker: Atharva Joshi
insights.so_what: FP8 gives only modest gains under weight streaming, implying transfer, not math, dominates on small cards.

insights.claim: Full 720p, 189-frame Cosmos 3 Nano text-to-video in BF16 took 2,624.9 s on an RTX 5070 (12 GB), 1,594.4 s on an RTX 5080 (16 GB), 1,052.2 s on an RTX 4090 (24 GB) and 1,016.7 s on an RTX 5090 (32 GB).
insights.speaker: Atharva Joshi
insights.so_what: VRAM capacity, not just architecture, drives local generative-video speed; supports upsell to higher-VRAM GPUs.

insights.claim: The prior-generation RTX 4090 with 24 GB nearly matched the RTX 5090 at 720p (1,052 s vs 1,017 s) and beat the 16 GB RTX 5080, indicating memory capacity matters more than GPU generation for streamed video-model inference.
insights.speaker: Atharva Joshi
insights.so_what: Suggests older high-VRAM cards retain value for local AI; NVIDIA cautions these are single-run results, not a controlled ranking.

insights.claim: Control-guided Transfer generation at 720p on an RTX 5070 took 4,834.9 s in BF16 (about 80 minutes) with guardrails off, the slowest modality, because Transfer performs more guidance work than text- or image-to-video.
insights.speaker: Atharva Joshi
insights.so_what: Local world-model generation remains batch, not interactive, on entry cards; cloud/data-center demand for production use persists.

insights.claim: NVIDIA recommends 12 GB GPUs start at 240p or 480p, 16 GB at 480p, while 24 GB gives materially faster full-resolution generation and 32 GB had the best measured consumer latency for 720p BF16.
insights.speaker: Atharva Joshi
insights.so_what: A clear VRAM-tier ladder for local AI video use cases.
